tldr: In cluttered environments, this bipedal MPC framework blends geometric obstacle-free corridors with Linear Inverted Pendulum capturability constraints. It mathematically guarantees that a feasible solution always exists, even with a prediction horizon as short as two steps.
hero_caption: Overview of the proposed framework. An axis-aligned safe corridor is generated offline or via global planning to avoid obstacles. Capturability-aware MPC (C-MPC) with recursive feasibility guarantees then runs across the sequence of overlapping rectangles. The planned footstep commands are tracked by the bipedal robot Digit using a 400 Hz whole-body controller (OSC-QP).
overview:
For humanoid robots to walk safely in cluttered environments built for humans, avoiding collisions with walls and furniture is not enough. They must also guarantee that they will not lose balance and fall over at the very next step. However, conventional safe corridor methods—which link obstacle-free spaces together as polyhedra—have mostly focused on purely geometric path planning without fully accounting for legged robot dynamics. As a result, when Model Predictive Control (MPC) is applied, there is an ever-present risk of infeasibility, where the optimization fails to find any valid control input.

To address this challenge, the authors focus on the Linear Inverted Pendulum (LIP) model, a widely used reduced-order model for bipedal locomotion, and embed capturability constraints (the ability to safely come to a complete stop within a finite number of steps) directly into rectangular safe corridors. Specifically, they analytically shrink each global safety rectangle to find an allowable footstep region that keeps the center of mass (COM) inside the bounds while preserving capturability. They also design a novel switching policy that checks whether a "Virtual Stopping Point" lies within the overlap between adjacent rectangles.

This design mathematically guarantees recursive feasibility across the entire corridor. In high-fidelity simulation tests with the humanoid robot Digit, the planner achieved a success rate of over 92% even when shrinking the prediction horizon to just two steps, with computation times on the order of a few hundred microseconds. Furthermore, when the robot encountered an unexpectedly closed door, it avoided an infeasible crash and autonomously transitioned into in-place stepping to safely wait, demonstrating strong fail-safe behavior.
contributions: Formulating an analytical contraction method to derive allowable footstep regions that guarantee capturability within geometric safety rectangles
Proving recursive feasibility across the entire safe corridor using a transition policy based on a "Virtual Stopping Point" that ensures safe stopping between rectangles
Achieving high success rates (92% to 94%) largely independent of prediction horizon length, enabling ultra-fast MPC solve times of just a few hundred microseconds
Demonstrating fail-safe behavior by autonomously switching to in-place walking when facing unforeseen blockages such as closed doors without prior knowledge

sections.heading: Finding where to step inside a bounded box without ever falling
sections.summary: For the Linear Inverted Pendulum (LIP) model, the authors analytically derive an allowable footstep rectangle that keeps the center of mass within a designated bounding box and guarantees safe stopping (capturability) within a finite number of steps. Formulating the MPC over this region ensures recursive feasibility within a single rectangle.
sections.details:
The Linear Inverted Pendulum (LIP) model is a standard tool in humanoid footstep planning, linearizing dynamics by maintaining a constant center-of-mass (COM) height. The motion of the LIP can be decoupled into a Divergent Component of Motion (DCM) and a Convergent Component of Motion (CCM). The set of states from which the robot can stop without falling is known as the $N$-step capturable basin.

### Computing allowable footstep rectangles that bound the COM
When avoiding obstacles, a safe rectangular bounding box $\mathcal{B}$ is geometrically defined to constrain where the COM can safely travel. However, simply enforcing that the COM stays inside $\mathcal{B}$ is not enough; the robot might fail to stop in time and collide with a wall or tip over. To prevent this, the proposed method analytically contracts $\mathcal{B}$ into a smaller footstep placement region $\mathcal{S}$. Placing footsteps $u$ within $\mathcal{S}$ guarantees that the robot can stop within at most $N$ steps while keeping the entire COM trajectory inside $\mathcal{B}$.

Specifically, by evaluating the upper and lower bounds of the COM position through the time-evolution equations of the DCM and CCM, the method directly derives the upper and lower footstep bounds $[\underline{w}, \overline{w}]$. This provides safety guarantees through simple rectangular clipping, without introducing complex nonlinear constraints.

### Recursively feasible MPC within a single rectangle
When foot placements are restricted to $\mathcal{S}$, the planner computes the maximum number of steps $\nu$ the robot can take in four directions (forward, backward, left, and right) before hitting the boundary. The MPC then incorporates a constraint requiring the DCM offset (the position of the DCM relative to the foot) to stay within this $\nu$-step capturable basin $\mathcal{C}_\nu$.

Thanks to this design, if the MPC has a feasible solution at the current step, it is mathematically guaranteed to remain feasible at the next step. In other words, as long as the robot stays within the rectangle, optimization infeasibility is provably eliminated.

captions.F2: (a) The LIP model moving on a constant plane along with the kinematic admissible footstep region (yellow). (b) Time evolution of COM trajectory (red), DCM (blue), and CCM (dashed orange), alongside the safe rectangle $\mathcal{B}$ (green) and the allowable footstep rectangle $\mathcal{S}$ (light blue). (c) The top-down view. By restricting foot placement $u$ within $\mathcal{S}$, the COM is guaranteed to stay within the outer safe rectangle $\mathcal{B}$ at all times.

sections.heading: Passing the baton between rectangles: switching via a Virtual Stopping Point
sections.summary: The authors introduce a fast algorithm to automatically generate a sequence of axis-aligned safe rectangles around obstacles, paired with a transition logic based on a "Virtual Stopping Point" that preserves capturability across rectangles. This completes the proof of recursive feasibility along the entire corridor.
sections.details:
A single rectangle is not enough for a robot to navigate through an entire room. To travel safely from start to goal, the planner must construct a "safe corridor" composed of overlapping rectangles and step from one to the next.

### Automatic generation of axis-aligned safe corridors
Using path waypoints obtained from a global path planner (such as JPS or RRT) as seed points, the algorithm searches for separating hyperplanes using the faces of rectangular obstacles. In Algorithm 1, by iteratively intersecting the half-spaces of the obstacles furthest from the seed point, the method rapidly generates collision-free, maximal axis-aligned rectangles $\mathcal{B}_i$. Chaining these together toward the goal produces a sequence of overlapping safe rectangles $\{\mathcal{B}_0, \ldots, \mathcal{B}_{M-1}\}$.

### Switching policy based on the Virtual Stopping Point
Conventional safe corridor methods rely on a purely geometric condition: "switch to the next MPC stage as soon as the COM enters the intersection of the two rectangles." However, under this rule, the robot might enter the next region with too much momentum, leaving it unable to brake before hitting the far wall of the new rectangle—meaning capturability is lost.

This is where the paper's key insight comes in. The authors define a "Virtual Stopping Point" $p^{\mathrm{stop}}$, which represents the final foot placement if the robot were to brake aggressively at maximum step length starting from its current foot position and DCM. The planner switches control to the next rectangle only when all three of the following conditions are met:
- The center of mass (COM) is within the intersection
- The current footstep position is within the intersection
- The Virtual Stopping Point $p^{\mathrm{stop}}$ is within the intersection

In other words, the planner passes the baton only after obtaining proof that the robot can come to a complete stop inside the next rectangle. Because this Virtual Stopping Point acts as a safety certificate, recursive feasibility remains unbroken even as the robot crosses between rectangles.

captions.F3: Automatic generation of obstacle-free rectangles using Algorithm 1. The planner iteratively identifies the furthest separating hyperplanes from each seed point relative to the obstacles and intersects their half-spaces to build collision-free local rectangles (red boxes).
captions.F4: Failed (left) and successful (right) switching checks between rectangles. Even if the COM (red) and footstep (yellow) enter the overlapping region, switching is denied and the robot decelerates if the Virtual Stopping Point $p^{\mathrm{stop}}$ (purple) lies outside. Only when $p^{\mathrm{stop}}$ is fully inside the intersection (right) does the planner safely switch to the next rectangle.

sections.heading: Step in place if a door is shut: testing short horizons and fail-safe motion
sections.summary: The method was evaluated across 100 randomized obstacle environments and in high-fidelity MuJoCo simulations of the Digit humanoid. The framework achieved an over 92% success rate with a horizon of just two steps, and successfully handled unexpected closed doors by autonomously transitioning into in-place walking to wait safely.
sections.details:
Simulations were conducted using the bipedal robot Digit. The high-level footstep MPC ran at 15 Hz, while low-level whole-body joint torque control (OSC-QP) operated at 400 Hz. The MPC was formulated using CasADi and solved with the lightweight OSQP solver.

### Benchmark comparison in randomized environments
The authors tested the method across 100 challenging environments, each measuring $50\,\mathrm{m} \times 50\,\mathrm{m}$ with 10 randomly placed rectangular obstacles, comparing it against a conventional corridor-based geometric MPC.
- **Success rate vs. horizon length**: While the conventional method required long prediction horizons $L$ to achieve viable success rates, the proposed method hit a 92% success rate with an extremely short horizon of $L=2$ (and 94% with $L=4$).
- **Computation time**: The MPC solved in roughly 150 $\mu\mathrm{s}$ at $L=2$ and about 220 $\mu\mathrm{s}$ at $L=5$. This is exceptionally fast, leaving plenty of headroom for the 15 Hz control loop.
- **Crucial difference in failure modes**: When the conventional method fails, it suffers from optimization infeasibility, leaving the robot uncontrollable. In contrast, failures under the proposed method only occurred in two benign modes: cases where the corridor could not form overlapping rectangles before execution (detected in advance), or narrow passages where the robot safely retreated into in-place stepping because safety could not be guaranteed. Instead of crashing, the system demonstrates graceful degradation.

### Office environment test with dynamic door opening and closing
In an office setting featuring three rooms and two doors, the robot walked without prior knowledge of when doors would open. The robot initially planned forward paths assuming all doors were open, but encountered a closed door along the way.

Because the next waypoint lay beyond the closed door, the MPC steered the COM toward a safe stop inside the current rectangle. The robot autonomously decelerated before the obstacle and began stepping in place, waiting safely in front of the door. As soon as the door opened, the safe rectangle expanded forward, allowing the robot to resume walking and reach its goal.

captions.F5: (a) Comparison of MPC success rates between the proposed method and the baseline. The proposed method (green) achieves a 92% success rate even with a horizon length of 2, safely falling back to in-place stepping (yellow) when it cannot advance. (b) MPC computation times of the proposed method, maintaining ultra-low latencies of 150 to 250 $\mu\mathrm{s}$ for horizons 2 through 5.

(b) Autonomously decelerating and stepping in place in front of the door while waiting for it to open. (c) Resuming forward walking after the door opens. (d) Overall corridor layout and planned trajectory. (e) Time history of COM velocity, showing that the robot slows to near zero (red box) to wait safely.

sections.heading: Wrap-up: how guaranteed capturability delivers real-time speed and safety
sections.summary: By integrating capturability into axis-aligned safe corridors, this work establishes recursive feasibility for bipedal footstep MPC in cluttered scenes. Drastically reducing the prediction horizon keeps computational overhead negligible, while autonomous in-place stepping provides a practical foundation for safe navigation during unexpected events.
sections.details:
This work elegantly bridges two domains that have often been treated in isolation: geometric corridor generation and control-theoretic capturability, connected through the intuitive yet rigorous concept of the Virtual Stopping Point.

The most practical benefit is that walking stability no longer relies on a long prediction horizon. With solve times kept within a few hundred microseconds, this footstep MPC can easily run on embedded microcontrollers and high-frequency loops. Moreover, when faced with unexpected environmental changes like a closed door, the optimization avoids divergence and naturally degrades into safe, in-place stepping—an essential fail-safe behavior for humanoids operating around people in the real world.

takeaways: Requiring the Virtual Stopping Point (the reachable terminal stopping footstep) to lie inside the overlap alongside the geometric corridor intersection mathematically guarantees recursive feasibility across transitions.
Embedding capturability constraints maintains long-term stability even with a prediction horizon as short as $L=2$, cutting MPC computation times down to hundreds of microseconds.
When optimization cannot proceed forward, gracefully degrading into safe in-place stepping rather than falling due to infeasibility is highly effective for practical robotics.
limitations: The current formulation relies on axis-aligned rectangular obstacles, which can lead to overly conservative corridors when dealing with angled walls or complex obstacle shapes.

Recursive feasibility is guaranteed only at the high-level LIP footstep planning layer; tracking failures at the low-level whole-body dynamics layer (such as joint torque limits or friction cone violations) are not theoretically ruled out.

If the overlap between adjacent rectangles is narrow and the target traversal speed is high, the Virtual Stopping Point may struggle to land within the intersection, forcing the robot to decelerate unnecessarily.
